## Probability distribution {background-image="image-main.png" auto-animate="true"}

Let us continue...

**Remember:** For $n$ independent trials with probability $p$:

$$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Question:** What shape do you notice as $n$ gets larger?
:::

Because of this pattern, we define what we called the **normal distribution**.

## Normal distribution {background-image="image-main.png" auto-animate="true"} 

A **normal distribution** is a continuous probability distribution that describes the population that has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ forms a bell-shaped curve.

## Normal distribution {background-image="image-main.png" auto-animate="true"} 

A **normal distribution** is a continuous probability distribution that describes the population that has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ forms a bell-shaped curve.

**Key characteristics:**

::: incremental
- Bell-shaped and symmetric
- Mean = Median = Mode (all at the center)
- Total area under curve = 1 (or 100%)
- Extends indefinitely in both directions (left and right of the mean $\mu$)
:::

## Normal distribution {background-image="image-main.png" auto-animate="true"} 

It has its own closed mathematical form that defines the normal distribution:

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\!\left( -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
$$

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
The $f(x)$ there refers to the density function. 
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
The random variable for this distribution $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)$ (reads as "x follows the normal distribution with parameters mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$"). 
:::

## Visualization of the normal distribution {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast" .scrollable} 

```{ojs}
//| panel: fill
viewof mu = Inputs.range([-7, 7], {
    label: "Mean (μ)",
    value: 0,
    step: 0.1
})

viewof sigma = Inputs.range([0.001, 5], {
    label: "Standard Deviation (σ)",
    value: 1,
    step: 0.01
})

{
    const width = 800;
    const height = 400;
    const margin = {top: 20, right: 30, bottom: 40, left: 50};
    
    const xMin = -10;
    const xMax = 10;
    
    const data = [];
    for (let x = xMin; x <= xMax; x += 0.1) {
        const y = (1 / (sigma * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))) * 
                  Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - mu) / sigma, 2));
        data.push({x, y});
    }
    
    const svg = d3.create("svg")
        .attr("width", width)
        .attr("height", height)
        .attr("viewBox", [0, 0, width, height]);
    
    const xScale = d3.scaleLinear()
        .domain([xMin, xMax])
        .range([margin.left, width - margin.right]);
    
    const yScale = d3.scaleLinear()
        .domain([0, 0.9])
        .range([height - margin.bottom, margin.top]);
    
    const line = d3.line()
        .x(d => xScale(d.x))
        .y(d => yScale(d.y));
    
    svg.append("path")
        .datum(data)
        .attr("fill", "none")
        .attr("stroke", "#4CAF50")
        .attr("stroke-width", 2.5)
        .attr("d", line);
    
    svg.append("g")
        .attr("transform", `translate(0,${height - margin.bottom})`)
        .call(d3.axisBottom(xScale));
    
    svg.append("g")
        .attr("transform", `translate(${margin.left},0)`)
        .call(d3.axisLeft(yScale));
    
    svg.append("line")
        .attr("x1", xScale(mu))
        .attr("x2", xScale(mu))
        .attr("y1", margin.top)
        .attr("y2", height - margin.bottom)
        .attr("stroke", "red")
        .attr("stroke-width", 2)
        .attr("stroke-dasharray", "5,5");
    
    return svg.node();
}
```

::: {.callout-note title="Observe"}
As you adjust $\mu$ and $\sigma$, notice how the curve shifts and spreads!
:::

## Characteristics of the normal distribution {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast" .scrollable} 

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Visual Properties

1.  **Bell-shaped** with highest peak at center
2.  **Symmetrical** about the mean
3.  **Continuous** on both sides
4.  **Horizontally Asymptotic** Never touches the horizontal axis

::::

## Characteristics of the normal distribution {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast" .scrollable} 

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Visual Properties

1.  **Bell-shaped** with highest peak at center
2.  **Symmetrical** about the mean
3.  **Continuous** on both sides
4.  **Horizontally Asymptotic** Never touches the horizontal axis

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Mathematical Properties

- Mean = Median = Mode
- Total area = 1 (100%)
- Determined by two parameters:
  - $\mu$ (mean): location
  - $\sigma$ (standard deviation): spread

::::
:::::

## Standard Normal Distribution {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast"}

The **standard normal distribution** is a special case where:

- Mean $\mu = 0$
- Standard deviation $\sigma = 1$

Most textbooks denotes the random variable $Z$ of the **standard normal distribution** as $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
We can scale down $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)$ to $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. We called it "**standardization**". 
:::

## The importance of z-scores {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast" .scrollable}

:::: columns

::: {.column width="25%"} 
### Compare different distributions

It is much easier to compare different distribution (still normal) on the same scale
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
### Dealing with probabilities

Although we have softwares for us to calculate such probabilities, interpreting probabilities under z-score scale is much easier. 
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Identify outliers

**Standardization** has a huge advantage to the application of outlier identification. 
:::

## The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule) {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast"}

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 800
#| components: [viewer]
box::use(
    shiny[
        sliderInput, radioButtons, hr, h4, textOutput, 
        plotOutput, uiOutput, renderPlot, renderText, 
        renderUI, shinyApp, HTML
    ],
    ggplot2[
        ggplot, aes, geom_line, geom_area, geom_vline, 
        theme_minimal, labs, 
        theme, element_text, linewidth
    ],
    bslib[page_sidebar, sidebar, card, card_header],
    stats[dnorm]
)

ui = page_sidebar(
    title = "Empirical Rule Interactive Visualization",
    sidebar = sidebar(
        sliderInput(
            "mean_val", "Mean (μ):", 
            min = -10, max = 10, value = 0, step = 0.5
        ),
        sliderInput(
            "sd_val", "Standard Deviation (σ):", 
            min = 0.5, max = 5, value = 1, step = 0.1
        ),
        radioButtons(
            "rule_select", "Show Rule:",
            choices = list(
                "68% Rule (±1σ)" = 1,
                "95% Rule (±2σ)" = 2,
                "99.7% Rule (±3σ)" = 3,
                "All Rules" = 4
            ),
            selected = 1
        ),
        hr(),
        h4("Current Values:"),
        textOutput("range_text")
    ),
    card(
        card_header("Normal Distribution Visualization"),
        plotOutput("normal_plot", height = "400px")
    ),
    card(
        card_header("Explanation"),
        uiOutput("explanation")
    )
)

server = function(input, output, session) {
    output$normal_plot = renderPlot({
        mu = input$mean_val
        sigma = input$sd_val
        rule = as.numeric(input$rule_select)
        
        x = seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 1000)
        y = dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
        
        df = data.frame(x = x, y = y)
        
        p = ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
            geom_line(color = "#2E86AB", linewidth = 1.5) +
            theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
            labs(x = "Value", y = "Density", 
                 title = "Normal Distribution with Empirical Rule") +
            theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))
        
        if (rule == 1 || rule == 4) {
            p = p + geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - sigma & x <= mu + sigma),
                              aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "#A23B72", alpha = 0.4)
        }
        
        if (rule == 2 || rule == 4) {
            p = p + geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - 2*sigma & x <= mu + 2*sigma),
                              aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "#F18F01", alpha = 0.3)
        }
        
        if (rule == 3 || rule == 4) {
            p = p + geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - 3*sigma & x <= mu + 3*sigma),
                              aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "#C73E1D", alpha = 0.2)
        }
        
        p = p + geom_vline(xintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed", 
                           color = "red", linewidth = 1)
        
        if (rule == 1 || rule == 4) {
            p = p + geom_vline(xintercept = c(mu - sigma, mu + sigma), 
                               linetype = "dotted", color = "#A23B72", linewidth = 1)
        }
        if (rule == 2 || rule == 4) {
            p = p + geom_vline(xintercept = c(mu - 2*sigma, mu + 2*sigma), 
                               linetype = "dotted", color = "#F18F01", linewidth = 1)
        }
        if (rule == 3 || rule == 4) {
            p = p + geom_vline(xintercept = c(mu - 3*sigma, mu + 3*sigma), 
                               linetype = "dotted", color = "#C73E1D", linewidth = 1)
        }
        
        p
    })
    
    output$range_text = renderText({
        mu = input$mean_val
        sigma = input$sd_val
        rule = as.numeric(input$rule_select)
        
        if (rule == 1) {
            paste0("68% of data falls between ", 
                   round(mu - sigma, 2), " and ", round(mu + sigma, 2))
        } else if (rule == 2) {
            paste0("95% of data falls between ", 
                   round(mu - 2*sigma, 2), " and ", round(mu + 2*sigma, 2))
        } else if (rule == 3) {
            paste0("99.7% of data falls between ", 
                   round(mu - 3*sigma, 2), " and ", round(mu + 3*sigma, 2))
        } else {
            paste0("μ ± 1σ: [", round(mu - sigma, 2), ", ", round(mu + sigma, 2), "]\n",
                   "μ ± 2σ: [", round(mu - 2*sigma, 2), ", ", round(mu + 2*sigma, 2), "]\n",
                   "μ ± 3σ: [", round(mu - 3*sigma, 2), ", ", round(mu + 3*sigma, 2), "]")
        }
    })
    
    output$explanation = renderUI({
        rule = as.numeric(input$rule_select)
        
        if (rule == 1) {
            HTML("<p><b>68% Rule:</b> Approximately 68% of all data values fall within 
           ONE standard deviation of the mean (μ ± σ).</p>")
        } else if (rule == 2) {
            HTML("<p><b>95% Rule:</b> Approximately 95% of all data values fall within 
           TWO standard deviations of the mean (μ ± 2σ).</p>")
        } else if (rule == 3) {
            HTML("<p><b>99.7% Rule:</b> Approximately 99.7% of all data values fall within 
           THREE standard deviations of the mean (μ ± 3σ).</p>")
        } else {
            HTML("<p><b>Complete Empirical Rule:</b> This shows all three rules simultaneously:
           <ul>
           <li>68% within μ ± σ (purple)</li>
           <li>95% within μ ± 2σ (orange)</li>
           <li>99.7% within μ ± 3σ (red)</li>
           </ul></p>")
        }
    })
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

## The Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule) {background-image="image-main.png" transition="fade" transition-speed="fast"}

The **Empirical Rule** (also called the **68-95-99.7 Rule**) tells us what percentage of data falls within certain distances from the mean in a normal distribution.

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="33%"}
### 68% Rule
Approximately **68%** of data falls within **1 standard deviation** of the mean:

$$\mu - \sigma \leq X \leq \mu + \sigma$$
::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}
### 95% Rule
Approximately **95%** of data falls within **2 standard deviations** of the mean:

$$\mu - 2\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma$$
::::

:::: {.column width="33%"}
### 99.7% Rule
Approximately **99.7%** of data falls within **3 standard deviations** of the mean:

$$\mu - 3\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 3\sigma$$
::::

:::::
